messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: School Counselor
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Stress: Stress, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells
  Maladaptive Strategies: Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Avoid Police: Police, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Vignette:
David sits in the chair, his hands clasped so tightly his knuckles are white. At thirty-four, he has the tired eyes of a much older man. For the past eight months, his life has been governed by a single, searing moment in time. He was driving home from the middle school where he works as a counselor, feeling the familiar weight of a stressful day. It was late autumn, that time of evening when the dusk and a steady drizzle conspire to blur the world into shades of grey. He remembers the chime of a text message, a quick glance down, and then the sudden, shocking thump against the front of his car. The memory never comes back as a simple recollection; it arrives as a complete sensory assault. The thin wall between then and now dissolves, and he is back in the driver’s seat, feeling the slick, cold steering wheel under his palms. He hears the awful sound again, sees the shape of the young woman crumpling onto the wet asphalt, and smells the rain mixing with something metallic and hot. It feels like it is happening right now, not like something that is over. When his wife asks him what’s wrong during these moments, he can only shake his head. He knows what happened, but the words to describe the horror of it are lost to him, caught somewhere in his throat.

The immediate aftermath was a blur of flashing lights and the sharp, antiseptic smell of the ambulance. That smell now haunts him in the most ordinary places; the hand sanitizer dispenser outside his office at school can send a jolt of panic through him, his heart beginning to hammer against his ribs as if trying to escape. He has come to believe that the accident was entirely his fault, a direct result of his own recklessness. This conviction, that "the event happened because of the way I acted," has become the central truth of his existence. It has poisoned his sense of self, especially at work. How can he, a man who made such a catastrophic error, guide young people through their own mistakes? He now doubts every decision he makes, certain that he can’t trust himself to do the right thing. When a student comes to him wrestling with a poor choice, David feels like a fraud, his advice hollow and hypocritical.

To survive, he has built a fortress of avoidance. He sold his car and now takes the bus, using a route that goes nowhere near the intersection where his life shattered. The sight of a police car sends a wave of nausea through him, and he will cross the street or duck into a shop to avoid passing one. At home, there is no silence. He constantly has podcasts or music playing, a wall of sound to keep his own thoughts at bay. He works late, volunteers for extra duties, anything to keep his mind occupied. This frantic activity has created a chasm between him and his wife. He sees her worry, but he cannot let her in. The guilt is a private, suffocating burden. At night, sleep offers no refuge. He lies awake for hours, convinced he needs to stay alert, though he doesn't know what for. He just feels a primal need to remain vigilant, as if another disaster is perpetually imminent.

The belief that his life has been destroyed by the trauma feels less like an opinion and more like a simple fact. The joy he once found in his marriage, his career, and his hobbies has been replaced by a constant, low-grade hum of fear and shame. The breaking point came last week during a routine dental cleaning. Lying back in the chair, the bright light in his eyes and the feeling of being unable to move triggered a full-blown panic attack. The hygienist’s gloved hands and the clinical smell of the room became the paramedics working on the woman in the street. He gasped for air, his body drenched in a cold sweat, overwhelmed by a sense of immediate and present danger. It was this experience—the utter loss of control in such a mundane setting—that finally forced him to seek help. David is here now because he cannot bear to live this way any longer, trapped in a single moment. He is terrified that he is permanently broken, but for the first time in months, he holds a fragile hope that he might one day find his way back to the man he was before the rain-slicked road and the terrible sound that changed everything.
